title: Your own iterators
description:
Implement `Iterator` for three types, and a function returning an iterator:

```rust
struct Collatz { next: Option<u64> }                    // Collatz::new(6) yields 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1
struct Primes { found: Vec<u64>, candidate: u64 }       // Primes::new() yields 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... forever
struct Chunks<'a, T> { data: &'a [T], size: usize }     // slices of `size` items; the last one may be shorter

fn digits(n: u64) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32>          // most significant digit first: 905 gives 9, 0, 5
```

`Chunks::new` panics for a size of 0. Since `Primes` is infinite, tests use `take`; `Primes` must test candidates only against the primes found so far, up to their square root.
hints: Each `next` call returns one value and updates the state for the following call; returning `None` ends the iterator. Every adapter (`take`, `count`, `max`...) then works for free.
`Chunks` hands out sub-slices of the original data: `split_at` divides the remaining slice into the chunk to return and the rest to keep.
